title: Development, Visualization, and Quantification of Mycobacterial Biofilms on Human Airway Epithelial Cells
author: Barclay, Limpens, et al.

In the next parts of the protocol, we describe several different methods to visualize and quantify biofilms formed on ALI-PBEC. Biomass of biofilms can be determined using crystal violet staining. Crystal violet stains mycobacteria and the extracellular matrix they produce. The optical density of the crystal violet staining is used to determine the total biomass of biofilms (Figure 1A). This staining should be performed on unfixed samples, at an appropriate biosafety level laboratory by trained staff following the local biosafety level restrictions. After staining, samples may subsequently be fixed for further microscopy analysis.CRITICAL: When staining biofilms attached to cells, the epithelial cells and the mucus produced are (partially) stained as well. Therefore, it is important to include uninfected control PBEC cultures for later background staining subtraction.Note: We normally use at least 3 technical replicates, i.e. separate ALI-PBEC wells of the same donor, per condition to reduce potential variation within this assay.6.After 24 h or 7 days of biofilm formation, remove bacterial suspensions from the apical side of ALI-PBEC, and the medium from the wells below inserts. Discard both medium and bacterial suspension.7.Wash ALI-PBEC apically to wash away non-adherent bacteria.a.Pipet 200 μL PBS at 18°C–21°C on the insert by placing the pipette against the side of the insert. Slowly allow the liquid to enter the apical side of the cells via the wall of the insert.b.Carefully remove supernatant from the inserts. Do not disturb the biofilms with the pipette tip.c.Repeat this washing step once more.Note: Mycobacterial biofilms, particularly those that are incubated for only 24 h, can be fragile. Be extremely careful while washing biofilms to prevent parts of the biofilm detaching from the cells.8.Stain adherent bacteria with crystal violet.a.Carefully add 200 μL of 1% crystal violet solution (Sigma-Aldrich) directly onto the cells of each insert, drop by drop. Do not pipette via the wall of the insert, as this may leave a residue that could interfere with the assay in step 10.b.Incubate for 10 min at 18°C–21°C.c.Remove crystal violet solution from each insert.9.Wash excess crystal violet solution from biofilms.a.Add 200 μL Milli-Q water to each insert by placing the pipette against the side of the insert.b.Carefully remove water with a pipette without disturbing biofilms.c.Repeat this washing step three times.10.Dissolve the crystal violet staining in ethanol.a.Add 200 μL 96% ethanol to each insert with a pipette.b.Incubate 10 min at 18°C–21°C.c.Transfer 100 μL from each insert to a clear 96-wells flat bottom plate.d.Prepare a 1:10 dilution of all samples in 96% ethanol.Note: Optical density of undiluted samples is likely too high (> 2.0) to accurately measure due to PBEC also being stained, although this depends on the detection range of the spectrophotometer used. Using a 1:10 or 1:100 dilution to measure optical density is required in this case.11.Measure optical density at 595 nm.12.Analyze results.a.Average OD595 values of technical replicates of uninfected control cultures.b.Subtract average uninfected control OD595 from all sample OD595 values.c.Multiply values by the dilution factor of the samples.Optional: Instead of dissolving and eluting crystal violet from the biofilm, stained biofilms can also be directly imaged using a light microscope. This technique works only for biofilms grown on transparent cell culture plates and not on biotic surfaces like PBEC, as crystal violet stains PBEC as well. To achieve this, perform the protocol until step 9c, and immediately image stained biofilms at 40–100 times magnification. steps.title: Prepare 7H9 broth
steps.instruction: Weigh 4.7 g 7H9 powder into a 1 L glass bottle, add 900 mL Milli‑Q water, 2 mL glycerol (final 0.2 % v/v) and 0.5 mL Tween‑80 (final 0.05 % v/v), invert to mix, autoclave, then cool to 45 °C.

steps.title: Make ADC supplement
steps.instruction: Dissolve 50 g BSA, 20 g dextrose and 0.03 g catalase in 1 L Milli‑Q water, filter through a 0.2 µm cellulose syringe filter, store at 2–8 °C (up to 3 months).

steps.title: Prepare 7H9 medium
steps.instruction: Add 100 mL ADC supplement to the cooled 7H9 broth (final ADC 10 %), store at 2–8 °C and use within 2 months.

steps.title: Prepare 7H10 agar base
steps.instruction: Weigh 19 g 7H10 agar into a 1 L bottle, add 900 mL Milli‑Q water and 5 mL glycerol (final 0.5 % v/v), invert to mix, autoclave and cool to 45 °C.

steps.title: Add OADC supplement to agar
steps.instruction: When the agar has cooled, add 100 mL Middlebrook OADC supplement (Thermo Fisher) to the agar solution.

steps.title: Dispense and set agar plates
steps.instruction: Pipet 35 mL of the agar into each sterile 10 × 10 cm square petri dish (≈28 dishes per litre), let set ≥12 h at 18–21 °C, then store plates at 2–8 °C (use within 2 months).

steps.title: Prepare cBD epithelial medium
steps.instruction: In a tissue‑culture cabinet, add 5 mL 100× penicillin/streptomycin to 500 mL BEpiCM‑b (final 1×). Separately, add 5 mL 100× penicillin/streptomycin, 12.5 mL 1 M HEPES (final 25 mM) and 5 mL 100× Glutamax to 500 mL DMEM. Mix 250 mL of each, add 5 mL BEpiCGS (final 1 %), aliquot 40 mL into 50 mL tubes and store at –20 °C (≤6 months) or 4 °C (≤4 weeks).

steps.title: Prepare 0.4 M cacodylic acid
steps.instruction: Add 950 mL Milli‑Q water to a 1 L bottle, weigh 86 g cacodylic acid, dissolve, adjust pH to 7.4 with HCl, bring volume to 1 L, store at 4 °C (≤6 months).

steps.title: Make 0.2 M cacodylic buffer
steps.instruction: Combine 5 mL of the 0.4 M cacodylic acid solution with 5 mL Milli‑Q water in a 50 mL tube.

steps.title: Add PFA to buffer
steps.instruction: Snap the lid of a 16 % PFA ampule and add 5 mL to the buffer (final 4 % PFA), mix well.

steps.title: Add glutaraldehyde to buffer
steps.instruction: Snap the lid of an 8 % GA ampule and add 5 mL to the same tube (final 2 % GA), mix, seal with parafilm and store at 4 °C (≤1 week).

steps.title: Prepare 0.1 M cacodylic storage buffer
steps.instruction: Mix 5 mL 0.4 M cacodylic acid with 14.38 mL Milli‑Q water in a 50 mL tube.

steps.title: Add PFA to storage buffer
steps.instruction: Snap a 16 % PFA ampule and add 0.62 mL to the tube from the previous step, mix, seal with parafilm and store at 4 °C (≤6 months).

steps.title: Remove bacterial suspension
steps.instruction: After 24 h or 7 days of biofilm growth, discard the apical bacterial suspension and the basal medium from each ALI‑PBEC insert.

steps.title: Wash inserts to remove non‑adherent bacteria
steps.instruction: Add 200 µL PBS (18–21 °C) to the apical side of each insert, let it flow along the wall, then carefully aspirate without touching the biofilm; repeat once more.

steps.title: Stain biofilm with crystal violet
steps.instruction: Add 200 µL of 1 % crystal violet solution (Sigma‑Aldrich) drop‑by‑drop onto each insert (avoid pipetting against the wall), incubate 10 min at 18–21 °C, then remove the stain.

steps.title: Wash excess crystal violet
steps.instruction: Add 200 µL Milli‑Q water to each insert, gently aspirate, and repeat the wash three times.

steps.title: Dissolve crystal violet for OD measurement
steps.instruction: Add 200 µL 96 % ethanol to each insert, incubate 10 min at 18–21 °C, transfer 100 µL to a clear 96‑well flat‑bottom plate, then dilute each sample 1:10 with 96 % ethanol.

steps.title: Measure optical density
steps.instruction: Read absorbance at 595 nm for each diluted sample.

steps.title: Analyze crystal violet data
steps.instruction: Average OD595 of technical replicates for uninfected controls, subtract this average from all sample ODs, then multiply by the dilution factor (10).

steps.title: Fix infected inserts with PFA
steps.instruction: Wash each insert with 0.5 mL PBS apically and 1.5 mL basal, add 500 µL 4 % PFA apically and 1 mL basally, seal plate edges with tape, and incubate ≥24 h at 4 °C.

steps.title: Remove fixative and store
steps.instruction: Wash inserts once with PBS (0.5 mL apical, 1 mL basal), add fresh PBS (same volumes), keep at 4 °C in PBS (use within 6 months or proceed immediately).

steps.title: Block membranes
steps.instruction: Wash inserts once with PBS (0.5 mL apical, 1 mL basal), then add 500 µL blocking buffer (1 % BSA, 0.3 % Triton‑X‑100 in PBS) apically and 1 mL basally; incubate 10 min at 18–21 °C or 30 min at 4 °C.

steps.title: Prepare primary EpCAM antibody
steps.instruction: In a light‑proof box with parafilm, dilute EpCAM stock (200 µg/mL) 1:20 in blocking buffer to 10 µg/mL, dispense 50 µL drops onto the parafilm.

steps.title: Excise membranes from inserts
steps.instruction: Invert each insert, cut around the membrane edges with a scalpel, and lift the membrane out.

steps.title: Incubate membranes with primary antibody
steps.instruction: Place each membrane (cells facing down) onto a 50 µL primary antibody drop, close the box lid, and incubate 1 h at 18–21 °C or 12–16 h at 4 °C in the dark.

steps.title: Prepare secondary antibody and WGA mix
steps.instruction: In a second parafilm‑lined box, dilute donkey‑anti‑goat Alexa Fluor 405 1:200 (from 2 mg/mL stock) to 10 µg/mL in blocking buffer, add wheat‑germ agglutinin 633 to a final 5 µg/mL (1:200 from 1 mg stock), dispense 50 µL drops.

steps.title: Wash membranes after primary incubation
steps.instruction: Fill three wells of a 6‑well plate with PBS, gently swing each membrane piece in the PBS three times, then discard the PBS.

steps.title: Incubate membranes with secondary/WGA
steps.instruction: Place membranes (cells facing down) onto the secondary‑antibody/WGA drops, seal the box, and incubate 2 h at 4 °C in the dark.

steps.title: Wash membranes after secondary incubation
steps.instruction: Fill three wells with PBS and three wells with Milli‑Q water; wash membranes three times in PBS then three times in water, gently swirling each time.

steps.title: Mount membranes on slides
steps.instruction: Blot a corner of each membrane on tissue paper, place membrane (cells up) on a glass slide, add a drop of anti‑fading reagent, cover with a coverslip, press to remove bubbles, let set 12–16 h at 18–21 °C, then store slides at 18–21 °C in a dark dry place (stable up to 3 months).

steps.title: Image membranes by confocal microscopy
steps.instruction: Using a confocal microscope (e.g., Leica SP8‑WLL, 40× oil immersion), acquire z‑stacks at 1 µm intervals through the ~30 µm thick sample; select images with strong bacterial fluorescence and minimal EpCAM signal.

steps.title: Quantify WGA polysaccharide staining
steps.instruction: Export the WGA channel from selected z‑stack images, open in Fiji, draw 50 × 50 µm ROIs (≥3 per insert), convert to binary with ‘Color Threshold’, analyse particles (minimum 3 px) to obtain fluorescent area, then sum pixel areas per ROI to get total WGA signal.

steps.title: Optional bacterial density quantification
steps.instruction: Repeat the ROI analysis on the bacterial fluorescence channel to estimate bacterial density within the biofilm.

description: Biofilm infections are notoriously difficult to eradicate and are often associated with recurrence and antibiotic resistance. Mycobacteria such as M. tuberculosis can also form biofilms in vitro and some studies suggest the presence of biofilms in vivo as well.2,3 Studying mycobacterial biofilm formation on a relevant mucosal surface such as the airway epithelium may provide insights in TB pathogenesis and improve treatment strategies. This protocol describes the steps to culture mycobacterial biofilms on air-liquid interface cultures of well-differentiated primary human bronchial epithelial cells (ALI-PBEC). Next, we describe steps to visualize and quantify the biomass of these biofilms via crystal violet staining. Furthermore, we provide instructions how to stain and quantify polysaccharides in the extracellular biofilm matrix secreted by mycobacteria. Finally, we illustrate how to prepare both planktonic mycobacteria as well as biofilms on ALI-PBEC cultured in a BSL-3 environment for scanning electron microscopy (SEM). With these techniques combined, biofilms of various mycobacterial species can be studied in detail. While the host surface used here for biofilm formation is the bronchial epithelium, these techniques may be transferrable to epithelial cultures from other regions, such as alveolar or nasal epithelium, as well. For detailed protocols to culture mycobacteria and ALI-PBEC, please refer to our related protocol in this issue of STAR Protocols, Barclay et al. (Barclay et al. co-submission 25-00065, this issue) and Ninaber et al.4
